title: Semantic Meaning & Best Practices 🏆
description: Write HTML that tells a story – not just a bunch of `<div>`s.

slides.title: Why Semantics Matter 🧠
slides.content:
# HTML That Explains Itself

Semantic HTML means choosing tags that describe their content. Instead of `<div class="header">` you can use `<header>`.
- **Accessibility:** Screen readers rely on semantics to navigate.
- **SEO:** Search engines better understand your page structure.
- **Maintainability:** Your code is easier to read and update.

A `<div>` has no meaning; a `<nav>` clearly says "this is navigation".

slides.title: Examples of Semantic Tags 🏷️
slides.content:
# Common Semantic Elements

- `<header>` – introductory content or navigational links.
- `<nav>` – primary navigation.
- `<main>` – dominant content of the page (only one per page).
- `<article>` – a self‑contained composition (blog post, news story).
- `<section>` – a thematic grouping of content.
- `<footer>` – footer of a page or section.

Full semantic coverage comes in Chapter 6, but start using these now!

quizData.question: Which tag should wrap the main navigation of a site?
quizData.explanation: <nav> is specifically for navigation blocks, giving meaning to assistive technologies.

slides.title: A Semantic Page Structure
slides.content: A typical webpage layout using semantic tags:
slides.codeSnippet:
My Blog

Home About

Post Title

Content goes here...

© 2025 My Blog

slides.title: Avoiding `<div>` Soup 🍜
slides.content:
# When to Use a `<div>`

`<div>` is not evil – it's a generic block container. Use it only when no semantic tag fits, like a wrapper for purely styling purposes.

❌ `<div class="nav">` → ✅ `<nav>`
❌ `<div class="article">` → ✅ `<article>`
❌ `<div class="footer">` → ✅ `<footer>`

Reserve `<div>` for purely presentational grouping.

quizData.question: It's okay to use <div> for a navigation menu if you add class="nav".
quizData.explanation: While it works, it's not semantic. Use the built‑in <nav> element; it provides meaning automatically.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Think in Outlines

Before coding, mentally outline your page: "header, navigation, main content, sidebar, footer". Then choose the semantic tag that matches each section. It's a habit that pays off forever.
